interventions.name: Decision Analysis
interventions.description: Decision analysis is a collaborative problem-solving technique in which the therapist helps the patient clarify her wishes and goals in a troubling interpersonal situation, generate a range of realistic alternative courses of action, and systematically evaluate the tradeoffs and interpersonal consequences of each option before acting. Because depressed patients often feel helpless, hopeless, and trapped in their circumstances—frequently believing they have no options at all—the therapist actively probes to elicit what outcome would make the patient happiest and what specific changes she wants from significant others. Only if the patient remains unable to generate new approaches despite leading questions does the clinician suggest additional alternatives not previously entertained, always emphasizing the patient's own agency and autonomy so that she internalizes decision analysis as an enduring interpersonal skill.
interventions.therapeutic_purpose: To help depressed patients overcome helplessness and passivity by clarifying their interpersonal wishes, expanding their perceived repertoire of action options, and weighing the realistic pros, cons, and tradeoffs of each choice prior to taking action.
when_to_use: When a patient faces an interpersonal problem, role dispute, or role transition and needs to consider alternative courses of action and their consequences

After communication analysis or encouragement of affect has clarified the patient's feelings and communication difficulties, as a bridge to selecting a new interpersonal strategy and rehearsing it in role play
When mobilizing a passive or chronically depressed patient who feels helpless or believes she has no options in dealing with an unfair situation or interpersonal transgression
When deciding whether, how, and to whom to express strong feelings (such as anger) or mobilize social supports in outside relationships
When helping primary care or medically ill patients problem-solve practical obstacles to treatment adherence, self-care, or medical regimen management
In adolescent depression prevention and treatment (IPT-A and IPT-AST) to build systematic interpersonal problem-solving skills
target_patterns: Depressive helplessness, passivity, and the subjective conviction that 'it hasn't felt like there were any options'
Difficulty identifying or prioritizing one's own interpersonal wishes, needs, and goals due to chronic self-effacement or guilt
Impulsive emotional action or, conversely, paralysis and avoidance when confronting interpersonal predicaments
Narrow or rigid problem-solving repertoires that overlook viable interpersonal alternatives or social supports
prerequisites: Clarification of the focal interpersonal problem and awareness of the patient's feelings and wishes regarding the situation
Sufficient affective regulation for the patient to delay impulsive action and reflect on consequences and tradeoffs
possible_questions: What would you want to happen?
What solution to this would make you happiest?
What are the alternatives?
What are the tradeoffs?
Have you considered all the choices?
What would you want him to do? What would be helpful to you? ... So what options do you have in dealing with Jack?
cautions: Always encourage the patient to think of solutions first through probing or leading questions before suggesting alternatives yourself; the goal is to foster the patient's own sense of agency and autonomy rather than doing things for her.
When offering advice, frame it as helping the patient consider options not previously entertained rather than giving direct suggestions or authoritarian commands.

When evaluating options for expressing strong anger outside the office, carefully weigh realistic cultural norms and relationship fragility so the chosen action does not endanger the patient or damage a fragile relationship.
expected_outcomes: Clear articulation by the patient of her own wishes, goals, and desired changes in a problematic relationship or life transition
Generation and realistic evaluation of multiple interpersonal options and their associated tradeoffs
Selection of a concrete, actionable interpersonal plan to rehearse via role play and implement between sessions
Internalization of decision analysis as a generalizable interpersonal skill that enhances autonomy and environmental control beyond termination

interventions.name: Interpersonal Role Playing
interventions.description: Interpersonal role playing is an active behavioral rehearsal technique used across all four IPT problem areas to help patients practice new ways of interacting, build interpersonal skills, and prepare for challenging encounters outside the office. Typically, the therapist takes the role of the significant other—often jumping directly into character without elaborate preamble so the exercise feels natural rather than like artificial playacting—and invites the patient to practice self-assertion, confrontation, limit-setting, or self-disclosure. In cases of interpersonal deficits, the patient may occasionally take the role of someone with whom she wishes to build a relationship, while in complicated bereavement, role play can take the form of an imaginary conversation with the deceased. Following each rehearsal, the clinician and patient evaluate both the verbal content ('Did you say what you wanted to say?') and the vocal delivery and tone ('How did you feel about your tone of voice?'), repeating the role play until the patient feels reasonably confident and planning contingencies for how the other person might interrupt, object, or react.
interventions.therapeutic_purpose: To clarify how the patient reacts to others and provide safe, iterative behavioral rehearsal of clear, assertive verbal content and appropriate vocal tone, building confidence and readiness to handle real-world interpersonal encounters and contingencies.
when_to_use: Across all four IPT problem areas to prepare the patient to interact differently, particularly in acting more assertively, setting limits, or expressing anger
In role disputes and role transitions to rehearse handling new situations or testing new ways to manage old, entrenched conflicts (including seeking an apology after an interpersonal transgression)
In complicated grief to conduct an imaginary conversation between the patient and the deceased significant other
In interpersonal deficits to practice self-disclosure and relationship-building skills, sometimes having the patient take the role of the person with whom she would like to develop a relationship

Extensively in persistent depressive disorder (IPT-D) to help chronically passive, risk-averse patients who have rarely expressed a wish or said 'no' become comfortable with self-assertion and confrontation

With depressed medical or college patients (e.g., socializing in nondrinking situations after a diabetes diagnosis) and in adolescent/preadolescent IPT (including dyadic parent-child sessions) to practice communication and peer or family problem-solving skills
target_patterns: Deficits in self-assertion, confrontation, limit-setting, or self-disclosure across interpersonal contexts
Incongruent, overly timid, or overly hostile tone of voice and delivery when attempting to express feelings or requests
Anxiety, trepidation, or avoidance regarding how a significant other will react (e.g., fear of being interrupted, blamed, or rejected)
Unresolved or unexpressed thoughts and feelings toward a deceased person in complicated bereavement
Social awkwardness or reliance on maladaptive coping (such as drinking) to navigate social or dating interactions
prerequisites: Identification of a specific interpersonal scenario, feeling, or message the patient wishes to communicate
Exploration of the patient's options (via communication and decision analysis) so the patient has a target approach to rehearse
possible_questions: But Deborah, I wanted to go to this movie!
Did you say what you wanted to say?
How did you feel about your tone of voice?
How did that sound? ... Is there something you would say differently? Did you say what you wanted to say? ... Were you happy with your tone of voice?
Let's talk about what you would specifically like Jack to do to help you out and also about how you can handle it if he should interrupt.
cautions: To avoid the role play feeling like artificial playacting, it is often helpful for the therapist to jump directly into the role of the other person, implicitly inviting the patient to respond.
Do not stop after a single pass if the patient remains shaky; repeat the role play until the patient feels reasonably confident with both the message content and the medium (tone of voice).

Always anticipate realistic contingencies—what might go wrong in the actual interchange (such as the partner becoming angry, denying, or cutting the patient off)—and rehearse how the patient can respond to those obstacles.
expected_outcomes: Increased clarity for both patient and therapist regarding how the patient reacts and comes across in interpersonal encounters
Greater patient confidence and satisfaction with both the verbal content and vocal tone of planned communications
Preparedness to handle interruptions, pushback, or unexpected reactions from significant others without retreating into silence or passivity
Successful execution of assertive communication, limit-setting, or social overtures outside therapy, reinforcing environmental mastery and symptom relief

interventions.name: Use of the Here-and-Now Therapeutic Relationship
interventions.description: While the primary focus of IPT remains squarely on the patient's relationships outside the office and IPT explicitly avoids psychodynamic transference interpretations, the therapist actively attends to the here-and-now therapeutic relationship as a vital foundation for treatment and an interpersonal arena in its own right. The clinician adopts the stance of a warm, authentic, nonjudgmental, hopeful ally and patient advocate. Because psychiatric patients are notoriously reluctant to criticize their clinicians, the IPT therapist explicitly invites the patient to voice negative feelings, complaints, apprehensions, or anger about the therapy or the therapist—and readily acknowledges and apologizes for genuine clinician mistakes (such as being late or mixing up an appointment). Addressing tensions or feedback directly in the present moment corrects interpersonal distortions, models constructive confrontation, and helps the patient experience herself as an active partner in treatment. In specific problem areas, the therapist also uses the dyadic relationship to give constructive feedback on how the patient comes across to others (in role disputes) or to serve as a direct, safe model for building outside relationships (in interpersonal deficits).
interventions.therapeutic_purpose: To maintain a strong, collaborative therapeutic alliance, model direct and non-defensive interpersonal communication, provide here-and-now feedback on how the patient comes across, and validate the patient's capacity to voice complaints and assert needs.
when_to_use: When difficulties, tensions, or negative feelings arise in the therapeutic relationship (e.g., the patient becomes angry at, feels criticized by, or dislikes something in the therapist's style)
When the therapist makes a mistake or is late to a session, requiring direct acknowledgment and a genuine apology
When patients new to psychotherapy feel uncomfortable with the therapeutic situation, question the therapist's credentials, or wish to end treatment early
In role disputes, to give the patient direct, nonjudgmental feedback on how she comes across to others and to illuminate maladaptive interaction styles
In interpersonal deficits, where the patient's relationship with the therapist provides a primary in-session model for interacting and building trust in outside relationships

When managing personality traits that complicate the alliance—such as disarming a mildly paranoid patient's suspiciousness with openness and optimal interpersonal distance, or gently encouraging independence and agency in a dependent patient who defers to authority

When consolidating the alliance with overburdened peripartum, adolescent, older adult, or medically hospitalized patients through flexible scheduling, telephone sessions, or brief practical assistance in early sessions
target_patterns: Aversion to criticizing authority figures or voicing legitimate complaints, apprehensions, and dislikes within a relationship
Interpersonal distortions or expectations of rejection/criticism occurring within the therapeutic dyad
Maladaptive interpersonal styles in role disputes or severe social isolation in interpersonal deficits that manifest in how the patient relates to the clinician
Excessive deference to authority and dependency, or guarded suspiciousness toward the clinician
Premature desire to drop out of treatment due to unvoiced alliance ruptures, discomfort with seeking help, or depressive hopelessness
prerequisites: Clinician authenticity, warmth, empathy, and willingness to act as the patient's non-neutral advocate against a depressive outlook and hostile environment
Clear professional boundaries (being warm and friendly without turning therapy into a social friendship or indulging therapist self-disclosure)
Non-defensive clinician readiness to accept criticism and apologize for real errors without interpreting patient complaints as childhood transference
possible_questions: Let's talk about what's going on between us. It's good that you're telling me you're upset—this is the sort of interpersonal communication we're working on, and with your feedback I can stop doing what's bothering you.
Are you feeling guilty about something? Ashamed? Fearful of what I might think about what's on your mind? Do you feel that something is inappropriate? That I'll disapprove?

Why do you want to stop at this point? If you want to end the treatment early, it's your choice, but we should consider why you do. ... Is there some problem between the two of us that we haven't discussed?
It's hard to get to treatment when you are feeling so bad and when you haven't slept and don't have much energy.
cautions: Do not exploit or interpret transference or link the patient's feelings toward the therapist to childhood antecedents or remote historical material; address all therapeutic relationship issues strictly in the here and now.
Do not keep the primary focus of treatment on the therapeutic dyad; the main focus of IPT must remain on the patient's relationships outside the office.
Maintain clear medical-model boundaries: being warm and friendly does not mean having a social friendship, and therapist self-disclosure is generally discouraged so the focus stays on the patient.

Do not adopt a neutral or silent stance when a patient is self-deprecating, as depressed patients interpret silence as agreement that they are worthless; actively attribute self-criticism and lateness to the depressive illness.

When reassuring a skeptical or uncomfortable patient that she may consider a different treatment or therapist without insulting you, do not present such nonchalance in offering a referral that the patient experiences you as uncaring or rejecting.

With a paranoid patient, avoid acting either too distant (and uninterested) or too intimate (and hence threatening); with a dependent patient, avoid accepting an authoritarian role or doing things for the patient that undermine her agency.
expected_outcomes: A robust, collaborative therapeutic alliance in which the patient feels understood, respected as a partner, and hopeful about recovery
Corrective in-session experience of voicing complaints, anger, or discomfort directly and having those feelings received non-defensively and constructively
Greater patient insight into how her interpersonal style comes across to others, alongside a healthy model for building outside relationships
Sustained treatment engagement and adherence to psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy across the time-limited course
